title: Passkeys and passwordless authentication
summary: Passkeys are FIDO2/WebAuthn credentials that replace passwords with public-key cryptography bound to a device or synced across a user's devices, resisting phishing and credential reuse.
whyItMatters: Passwords and one-time codes are widely targeted by phishing and credential stuffing. Passkeys remove the shared secret from the login flow, which can reduce phishing exposure and password-reset workload, but they force a rethink of enrollment, recovery and lost-device processes.
risks: Account recovery can become the weakest link
Synced passkeys shift trust to the credential manager or platform provider
Legacy applications keep passwords alive in mixed estates
Attestation and assurance needs differ for regulated use cases
User enrollment lags availability: being offered passkeys does not mean users adopt them

title: Identity-centric zero trust
summary: Zero trust treats identity as a primary control plane: every access request is authenticated, authorized and evaluated in context rather than trusted because of network location.
whyItMatters: Perimeter assumptions break down with cloud, SaaS and remote work. Identity-centric policy decisions let organizations apply least privilege per request, but they depend on accurate identity data, strong authentication and policy enforcement across applications.
risks: Poor identity data quality weakens policy decisions
Legacy applications without modern authentication cannot enforce per-request policy
Unclear ownership between network, identity and endpoint teams
Zero trust used as a label without measurable maturity goals

title: Identity threat detection and response (ITDR)
summary: ITDR is an industry label for monitoring identity systems, sessions and entitlements for attack behavior such as credential abuse and privilege escalation, and for supporting containment and response.
whyItMatters: Attackers can operate with valid accounts and abuse credentials (MITRE ATT&CK T1078), so controls focused only on prevention can miss them. ITDR adds detection and response tied to identity context. It is an industry label rather than a defined standard, so its scope varies by vendor.
risks: Scope and definition of ITDR vary between vendors and analysts
Detection depends on complete identity-provider and directory logging
Alert volume without tested response playbooks
Overlap with SIEM, EDR and PAM tooling

title: Non-human identity (NHI) security
summary: Non-human identities such as service accounts, API keys, tokens and workload identities are numerous, frequently over-privileged and long-lived, and often lack clear ownership or rotation.
whyItMatters: Machine credentials are embedded in code, pipelines and SaaS integrations where human-centric controls do not reach. Inventory, ownership, short-lived credentials and workload attestation change how identity programs are scoped.
risks: Secrets leaked in code repositories, logs and tickets
Long-lived credentials that are never rotated
No named owner for service accounts and integrations
Retrofitting workload identity into legacy systems
keyStandards: OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025, incubator project)

title: Identity governance (IGA) modernization
summary: Identity governance pairs account lifecycle management with recurring access reviews, which NIST SP 800-53 expects (AC-2). Products now add automation and review recommendations, such as inactive-user suggestions, to cut manual review effort.
whyItMatters: Joiner-mover-leaver errors and accumulated access can cause audit findings and excess privilege. Automation depends on clean authoritative data: vendor documentation itself notes the case where HR data is not in the identity system. Coverage of SaaS and non-human accounts is an open challenge for many programs.
risks: Poor authoritative-source data undermines automation
Reviewers approve in bulk without context (review fatigue)
Connector coverage gaps for SaaS and custom applications
Role mining projects that stall
keyStandards: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Access Control (AC) family

title: Just-in-time privileged access
summary: Privileged access management is moving from standing admin rights toward just-in-time, time-bound elevation with session monitoring and credential vaulting, shrinking the window in which privilege can be abused.
whyItMatters: Standing privileged access is a high-value target. Granting elevation only when needed, with approval and logging, supports least privilege (NIST SP 800-53 AC-6) and reduces exposure, at the cost of workflow friction and the need to plan emergency access.
risks: Approval friction pushes admins toward workarounds
Break-glass accounts are poorly protected or untested
Shadow privileged accounts outside the PAM inventory
Elevation workflows are not integrated with ticketing and change control
keyStandards: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 Least Privilege

title: Cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM)
summary: CIEM analyzes effective permissions across cloud accounts to find unused or excessive access and recommend least-privilege policies.
whyItMatters: Cloud permission models are granular and change quickly, so granted access drifts far from what is used. Tooling that compares granted and used permissions helps right-size access, though it works best alongside governance and infrastructure-as-code practices.
risks: Recommendations applied without testing can break workloads
Multi-cloud views are inconsistent between providers
Findings pile up without an owner or remediation process
Console changes bypass infrastructure-as-code

title: Decentralized identity and digital identity wallets
summary: Verifiable credentials and digital identity wallets let people hold signed attestations and present them selectively, reducing reliance on centralized identity providers for some use cases.
whyItMatters: Reusable, cryptographically verifiable credentials could simplify onboarding and proofing and improve privacy through selective disclosure. Ecosystem trust frameworks, wallet interoperability and issuer adoption are still maturing. The FIDO Alliance is developing a digital identity wallet certification program, and the W3C Verifiable Credentials Working Group is drafting threat models and a revocation status mechanism (Bitstring Status List v1.1).
risks: Interoperability between credential formats and wallets
Unclear trust frameworks and issuer accreditation
Credential revocation and recovery are hard problems
Low relying-party adoption limits user value

title: Identity for AI agents
summary: AI agents act on behalf of users and call tools and APIs, raising new questions about how to identify, authenticate, authorize, delegate to and audit autonomous software actors.
whyItMatters: Agents can chain actions across systems using delegated credentials, which strains models built for human sessions and static service accounts. The OpenID Foundation has published a threat model for agents that cross security boundaries, and agent-initiated payments raise the question of what the user has authorized the agent to do. Scoped, short-lived, auditable delegation is an active area of standards and product work.
risks: Over-broad delegated tokens give an agent more access than the task needs
Prompt injection can turn legitimate agent access into misuse
Weak attribution of agent actions in audit logs
Agents crossing security boundaries between providers or organizations
Standards and protocols are still changing

title: Identity-related regulation and standards
summary: Regulation increasingly sets identity and access expectations, including NIS2 and DORA in the EU, eIDAS amendments for digital identity wallets, and evolving NIST digital identity guidelines in the US.
whyItMatters: Compliance drives requirements for strong authentication, access governance and third-party access control. Obligations and deadlines differ by sector and jurisdiction and change over time, so teams should map them to their own scope rather than rely on summaries.
risks: Misreading which obligations apply to your entity and sector
Evidence for access controls is scattered across tools
Deadlines and national transposition vary by jurisdiction
Treating compliance as the ceiling for identity security
